Chapter 3 · 第三章

Building Relationships建立与经营人际关系

— PDF p.75 —

Everyone in tech understands the value of networking when it comes to advancing their career. It's how you hear about job openings before they're public, skip the application line with referrals, or even land promotions by building trust with managers. Networking gets you insider knowledge about companies, helps you decide if they're the right fit, and gives you a direct line to opportunities that might otherwise take years to stumble upon. The right relationships can fast-track your career and save you from a lot of wasted time and effort.

在科技行业，人人都懂得拓展人脉对职业发展的价值。靠人脉，你能在职位公开前就听到招聘消息，靠内推跳过排队投递，甚至靠与经理建立信任而获得晋升。人脉让你获得公司的内部信息，帮你判断它是否适合自己，还能让你直接触达那些原本可能要好几年才偶然碰到的机会。合适的关系能让你的职业快车道起来，帮你省去大量浪费的时间和精力。

As a tech lead, the stakes are even higher. Building strong relationships isn't just about you anymore; it directly impacts your team and the teams you collaborate with. The benefits multiply significantly, from creating smoother workflows to opening doors to new opportunities for your team. Yet, I've noticed many tech leads roll their eyes when I bring this up. They see building relationships as time wasted, a distraction from coding, and often fail to connect the dots between stronger relationships and fewer headaches for themselves and their team.

作为技术负责人，这件事的赌注更高。经营牢固的关系不再只关乎你自己；它会直接影响你的团队以及与你协作的其他团队。回报会成倍放大——从让协作流程更顺畅，到为你的团队打开新机会的大门。然而我注意到，很多技术负责人一听到这个话题就翻白眼。他们把经营关系看成浪费时间、是写代码之外的分心，常常看不到更牢固的关系与自己和团队更少头疼之间的关联。

This chapter is here to change the perception that building relationships is a waste of time. I'll show you the value of investing in the right relationships as a tech lead and how these connections can unlock opportunities, prevent unnecessary problems, and make life easier for everyone involved. I'll dive into the relationships you need to focus on, strategies for building and maintaining them, and ways to overcome common struggles like breaking the ice with someone new, keeping relationships strong over time, and connecting with nontechnical people in other departments.

本章要做的，就是改变“经营关系是浪费时间”这种看法。我会向你展示，作为技术负责人，投资于恰当的关系有多大价值，这些关系又如何能打开机会、本可避免的问题，并让所有相关人的日子都更好过。我会深入讲你需要重点经营哪些关系、建立与维护这些关系的策略，以及如何克服常见难题：如何与陌生人破冰、如何让关系长期保鲜、如何与其他部门的非技术同事建立连接。

The Value of Building Strong Relationships建立牢固关系的价值

One of the teams I led stood out as one of the most successful I've worked with, not just in terms of results but in how we worked together. We delivered reliably, collaborated efficiently across teams, handled conflict in healthy ways, and brought in significant business value. People were happy and proud to be part of it. I'm convinced that one of the biggest reasons for this team's success was the relationships we built, with each other, with stakeholders, and with clients. These relationships didn't just happen on their own. As a tech lead, I made them a deliberate focus. I didn't wait and hope connections would form naturally; I put consistent effort into building and nurturing them every step of the way.

我带过的一支团队，是我合作过的最成功的团队之一——不仅看结果，也看我们协作的方式。我们交付稳定、跨团队协作高效、以健康的方式处理冲突，并带来了可观的业务价值。大家都乐在其中、为身为团队一员而自豪。我深信这支团队成功的最大原因之一，就是我们所建立的关系——彼此之间、与干系人之间、与客户之间。这些关系不是自然而然发生的。作为技术负责人，我有意把它们当作重点。我没有干等着、指望关系会自然形成；而是在每一步都持续投入精力去建立和滋养它们。

— PDF p.76 —

Within the team, we created a space where tough conversations could happen without hesitation. When something came up, we addressed it head-on, tackling issues quickly instead of letting them grow into bigger problems. We challenged each other constructively, not to prove someone wrong but to help everyone grow. Feedback became a daily improvement tool for us. Decision making wasn't just up to me; we debated ideas openly, came to agreements together, and took collective ownership. It wasn't always easy, but it set us apart as a cohesive and high-performing team. If you're curious about how we created this environment, the section “How to Create Psychological Safety on Your Team” on page 188 dives deeper into the specific practices we used.

在团队内部，我们营造了一个可以毫无顾虑地进行艰难对话的空间。问题一出现，我们就正面迎上，快速处理，而不是让它发酵成更大的麻烦。我们以建设性的方式互相挑战，不是为了证明谁错，而是为了帮助每个人成长。反馈成了我们日常改进的工具。决策不只由我一个人定；我们公开讨论想法、共同达成一致，并集体承担责任。这并不总是轻松，但它让我们成为一支有凝聚力、高绩效的团队。如果你好奇我们是如何营造这种环境的，第 188 页“如何在团队中建立心理安全感”一节会更深入地介绍我们用过的具体做法。

Building strong relationships with stakeholders, especially on the client side, gave my team a huge advantage. I invested in these relationships consistently, showing up for them in ways that mattered: whether it was being transparent about potential issues, helping them prepare for tough conversations, or stepping up to support initiatives outside my immediate responsibilities, like writing stories or contributing to their ideas.

与干系人（尤其是客户方）建立牢固关系，给我的团队带来了巨大优势。我持续投资于这些关系，以真正有分量的方式出现在他们面前：无论是对潜在问题保持透明、帮他们为艰难对话做准备，还是主动承担起职责范围之外的事来支持他们的项目，比如写用户故事、为他们的想法出力。

A great example is advocating for addressing tech debt. Many tech leads struggle to convince stakeholders to prioritize it because it's often perceived as wasted time on the business side. But thanks to the trust I built with our product manager, he didn't need convincing. He trusted our judgment because of the foundation we had built, and when I asked for time to clean up a feature toggle to avoid confusing code that might slow down future reviews or increase the risk of bugs, or address technical debt more broadly, he didn't hesitate to say yes, even if he didn't fully understand the technical details. That trust came from consistent effort: recurring one-on-ones, full transparency around progress and potential risks, and staying responsive even when things got tough.

一个很好的例子是推动处理技术债。很多技术负责人很难说服干系人优先处理技术债，因为业务方往往觉得这是在浪费时间。但多亏了我和产品经理之间建立的信任，他根本不需要被说服。因为有我们打下的基础，他信任我们的判断；当我申请时间去清理一个特性开关（以免留下令人困惑的代码、拖慢未来的评审或增加出 bug 的风险），或更广泛地处理技术债时，他毫不犹豫就答应了——哪怕他并不完全懂技术细节。这份信任来自持续的投入：定期一对一、对进展和潜在风险完全透明，以及即使情况棘手也始终保持响应。

Here is another example of how building a strong network and staying visible as a team can pay off: when an exciting opportunity came up, like leading a high-profile product launch, we were the first team considered and offered the chance to develop the project because we had consistently stayed visible and well-connected.

再举一个例子，说明建立牢固的人际网络、让团队持续保持“可见度”如何带来回报：当一个令人兴奋的机会出现时——比如主导一次高关注度的产品发布——我们是第一个被想到、并被委以项目开发的团队，原因就是我们一直保持着可见度、且人脉畅通。

— PDF p.77 —

When working with other teams, building relationships allowed us to share knowledge and collaborate more effectively. Knowing what they were working on helped us avoid duplicating effort and saved us a lot of time. At the same time, we made sure our work was visible by offering solutions we'd already implemented to others, which built our reputation across the company.

在与其他团队协作时，建立关系让我们能够共享知识、更高效地协作。了解他们在做什么，帮我们避免了重复劳动，省下大量时间。与此同时，我们也通过把已经落地的方案分享给别人，让自己的工作被看见，从而在全公司积累了口碑。

Every time I share these stories and the benefits of strong relationships with tech leads, one question comes up again and again: “If I do all of these, when do I do my job?”

每次我把这些故事和牢固关系的好处讲给技术负责人听，总有一个问题反复出现：“如果这些都要做，我什么时候才做自己的本职工作？”

Building relationships isn't something separate from your job. It is your job.

经营关系并不是你本职工作之外的事。它本身就是你的本职工作。

The good news is, you don't have to do it all on your own. One of the best ways to build a connected, resilient team is to involve others. Delegate. Empower your team to represent and support one another. For example, you might have a staff engineer lead guild meetings or ask a team member to attend a cross-functional sync.

好消息是，你不必事事亲力亲为。打造一支彼此连接、有韧性的团队，最好的办法之一就是让别人也参与进来。授权。让你的团队有能力互相代表、互相支持。比如，你可以让一位资深工程师主持技术社区（guild）会议，或者请某位团队成员去参加跨部门同步会。

In my case, I encouraged my team to build their own bridges by visiting clients, collaborating with peers in other teams, and being proactive in communication. We set up open Slack channels, made ourselves available, and made clarity a priority. Even if it felt repetitive, we over-communicated to ensure everyone stayed aligned.

就我自己的做法而言，我鼓励团队自己去搭建桥梁：走访客户、与其他团队的同行协作、主动沟通。我们开设了公开的 Slack 频道、让自己随时可联系、并把“讲清楚”当作优先事项。哪怕显得重复，我们也宁可沟通过度，以确保所有人都保持对齐。

Strong relationships don't just depend on you; they're a shared effort. And yes, this work takes time and energy. But the payoff is real: fewer misunderstand-ings, smoother collaborations, a team that's more motivated and empowered to deliver their best work (Figure 3-1).

牢固的关系不只靠你一个人；它是大家共同的努力。是的，这件事要花时间和精力。但回报是实实在在的：误解更少、协作更顺畅、团队更有动力、也更有能力交付最好的成果（图 3-1）。

As a tech lead, you're responsible for developing an environment where people feel safe to speak up, collaborate openly, and trust each other. You may not always be able to predict exactly how or when a strong relationship will help, but it will. The effects ripple through your team's work in ways that matter. It's an investment you and your team make together, and one that always pays off.

作为技术负责人，你有责任打造一个让大家敢于发声、开放协作、彼此信任的环境。你未必总能预料到一段牢固的关系会在何时、以何种方式帮上忙，但它一定会帮上忙。它的影响会以重要的方式扩散到团队的工作中。这是你和团队共同做出的一笔投资，而且总有回报。

— PDF p.78 —

How to Build Strong Relationships如何建立牢固的关系

At the core of any meaningful connection is trust, and trust is built through four foundational practices:

任何有意义的关系，其核心都是信任；而信任靠四项基础实践来建立：

  • Effective communication — Making sure your message lands as intended and that you're also hearing others clearly.有效的沟通——确保你的信息按预期传达出去，同时你也清楚地听懂了别人。
  • Consistent communication — Staying in touch regularly.持续的沟通——保持定期联系。
  • Transparent communication — Sharing openly, including uncertainties, trade-offs, and the “why” behind decisions.透明的沟通——开诚布公地分享，包括不确定性、权衡取舍，以及决策背后的“为什么”。
  • Follow-through — Doing what you say you'll do and showing you can be counted on.说到做到——答应的事就去做，证明你值得依靠。

Each of these practices reinforces the others. When you communicate clearly, frequently, and honestly, and back it up with action, trust builds natu-rally. In this section, I'll break these down one by one.

这四项实践彼此强化。当你清晰、频繁、诚实地沟通，并用行动做后盾，信任就会自然建立起来。本节我会逐一展开。

But before we dive into these practices, I want to call out one thing that I believe is a game-changer when it comes to building trust quickly: meeting people face-to-face.

但在深入这些实践之前，我想先点出一件我认为能快速建立信任的“胜负手”：与当面对人见面。

There's something about human connection that no tool or strategy can fully replicate. Face-to-face interaction speeds up trust in a way that's hard to explain but easy to feel. That doesn't mean I'm advocating for full-time in-person work; I've been working remotely for years. But if you have the chance to meet someone in person, take it.

人与人之间当面建立的连接，有某种东西是任何工具或策略都无法完全复制的。面对面互动能加速信任的建立，这种效果很难解释，却很容易感受到。这并不是说我主张全职坐班；我自己远程工作很多年了。但如果你有机会和某人当面见一面，就抓住它。

It could be a team lunch on a day when everyone's in the office, a coffee with a stakeholder, an offsite that brings people together, or even a celebration for a big release. These moments of shared presence can set a foundation that makes every future interaction smoother, more human, and more effective, even once you're back to Zoom calls and Slack threads.

它可以是大家都到办公室那天的团队午餐、和某位干系人喝杯咖啡、一次把大家聚到一起的外出团建，甚至是一次为重要发布办的庆祝。这些共同在场的时刻能打下一个基础，让此后的每一次互动都更顺畅、更有人情味、也更高效——即便之后又回到 Zoom 会议和 Slack 串聊。

This being said, I do know that these in-person moments aren't always possi-ble, and that's OK. What matters most is how you show up in every interaction.

话虽如此，我也知道这些当面时刻并不总能实现，这没关系。最重要的是你在每一次互动中如何登场。

— PDF p.79 —

Whether remote or in person, the following practices will help you build strong, lasting relationships grounded in trust.

无论远程还是当面，下面这些实践都能帮你建立以信任为基础、牢固而持久的关系。

Communicate Effectively有效沟通

Effective communication is the foundation beneath everything else. You can be consistent and transparent, but if your message doesn't land, or you misunder-stand others, trust starts to erode.

有效沟通是一切之下的根基。你可以持续、透明，但如果信息传不出去，或者你误解了别人，信任就会开始侵蚀。

And in order to really understand, you need to really listen. Here are some strategies to develop your active listening skill:

而要真正理解别人，你需要真正去倾听。下面是一些培养积极倾听能力的策略：

  • Focus fully on the speaker — Give them your full attention. Silence notifications, minimize distractions, and resist the urge to plan your response while they're speaking. This simple shift shows respect and reinforces that you're present.全神贯注于说话者——把全部注意力交给对方。关掉通知、减少分心，别在对方说话时就琢磨自己怎么回应。这个小小的转变既表达尊重，也表明你在场。
  • Get comfortable with silence — Pause before responding; counting to some fixed number can help (even briefly holding your comment) and give space for reflection or additional thoughts from the speaker.学会与沉默共处——回应之前先停顿；在心里数几个数会有帮助（哪怕只是短暂地压住自己的话头），给对方留出反思或补充想法的空间。
  • Reflect to confirm your understanding — Use phrases like “Did I get that right?” or “Let me try to rephrase what I heard…” to ensure clarity and avoid misunderstandings.复述以确认你的理解——用“我理解得对吗？”或“让我把听到的复述一遍……”这样的说法，确保清晰、避免误解。
  • Use open-ended questions — Encourage deeper responses with prompts like “Please tell me more about that…” or “What's your perspective on…?”使用开放式问题——用“再多跟我讲讲那件事……”或“你对此怎么看？”这类引导，鼓励对方给出更深入的回答。
  • Reflect after conversations — Post-discussion, ask yourself: How well did I listen? Did my mind wander? Did I interrupt? This helps build self-awareness over time.对话后复盘——聊完之后问自己：我听得有多投入？我走神了吗？我打断别人了吗？这会随着时间帮你建立自我觉察。
  • Seek feedback on your listening — Ask team members directly, “What's one thing I could do to make you feel more heard?” This input is invaluable for growth.就你的倾听征求反馈——直接问团队成员：“我做哪一件事，能让你觉得自己的话被更好地听进去了？”这种反馈对成长极为宝贵。

So aim to listen not just for information but for understanding. Then, when it's your turn to share, follow these guidelines:

所以，倾听的目标不应只是获取信息，而是理解对方。那么，轮到你表达时，请遵循以下原则：

  • Be clear — Use simple, direct language.清晰——使用简单、直接的语言。
— PDF p.80 —
  • Be structured — Bullet-point key takeaways. Add summaries when things get long.有条理——用项目符号列出要点；内容变长时加上小结。
  • Be considerate — Tailor your message to the audience: what do they need to know?体谅对方——根据受众裁剪信息：他们需要知道什么？
  • Be helpful — Link to docs, add examples, or suggest next steps.有帮助——链接到文档、补充示例，或给出下一步建议。
  • Be reflective — Take a second before you speak or write. Don't just dump your thoughts as they come.先想后说——开口或动笔前停一秒。不要想到什么就把想法一股脑倒出来。

AI assistants can be surprisingly effective at helping you with this, especially because they provide a low-pressure environment for practice, feedback, and iteration. Here's how they can support you:

AI 助手在这件事上能出奇地有效，尤其因为它们提供了一个低压环境，供你练习、获得反馈和反复迭代。它们可以这样帮你：

  • Practice difficult conversations — Simulate one-on-one conversations or challenging scenarios, like giving feedback, handling disagreement, or delivering bad news. Prompt: “Act as a team member who's unhappy with a project decision. Help me practice how to respond in a calm and clear way.”演练艰难对话——模拟一对一或有挑战的场景，比如给出反馈、处理分歧、传达坏消息。提示词示例：“扮演一位对某项项目决策不满的团队成员，帮我练习如何冷静、清晰地回应。”
  • Improve written communication — Paste your Slack message, status update, or email and ask the AI to check for tone, clarity, and simplicity. You can even request a rewrite tailored to your audience (e.g., nontechnical stakeholders, busy execs). Prompt: “Rewrite this status update to make it more concise and less technical.”改善书面沟通——把你的 Slack 消息、进展更新或邮件贴进去，让 AI 检查语气、清晰度和简洁度。你甚至可以要求它按你的受众（比如非技术干系人、忙碌的高管）重写。提示词示例：“把这份进展更新改写得更简洁、少些技术味。”
  • Ask for structure and models — AI can help you organize complex ideas into clear, easy-to-understand formats, like Problem–Solution–Impact or Before–After–Benefit. Try prompting “I need to explain a complex idea to my manager. Can you help me structure it in a way that's easy to understand?”请它帮你组织结构和模板——AI 能帮你把复杂想法整理成清晰易懂的格式，比如“问题—方案—影响”或“之前—之后—收益”。可以试试这样提问：“我要向经理解释一个复杂想法，你能帮我把它组织成容易理解的结构吗？”
  • Get feedback on tone and intent — AI can help you assess whether your message might come across as harsh, vague, or passive. This is especially useful when you're unsure how it might land. Prompt: “Here's what I wrote; does it sound defensive?”就语气和意图获取反馈——AI 能帮你判断信息听起来是否会显得生硬、含糊或被动。当你拿不准信息传出去会怎样时，这尤其有用。提示词示例：“这是我写的，听起来有防御性吗？”
— PDF p.81 —
  • Learn by doing — Ask AI to analyze communication examples and suggest improvements so you can learn patterns over time. Prompt: “What makes this message confusing? How would you improve it?”在做中学——让 AI 分析沟通案例并提出改进建议，这样你就能逐渐总结出规律。提示词示例：“这条消息为什么让人困惑？你会怎么改？”

Communicating well is a skill, and like any skill, it can be learned and refined over time. The better you get at this, the easier it becomes to build trust, influence outcomes, and keep your team aligned, especially in high-pressure moments.

良好的沟通是一项技能，和任何技能一样，它可以通过学习和长期打磨而精进。你越擅长沟通，就越容易建立信任、影响结果、让团队保持对齐——尤其是在高压时刻。

Tip. If you want to go deeper into communication strategies that help build strong relationships, I definitely recommend Nonviolent Communication, a system developed by Marshall B. Rosenberg. You can learn more through his book with the same title, published by PuddleDancer Press, and there are other resources available through the Center for Nonviolent Communication.提示。如果你想深入学习那些有助于建立牢固关系的沟通策略，我强烈推荐《非暴力沟通》（Nonviolent Communication），这是 Marshall B. Rosenberg 发展出的一套体系。你可以通过他由 PuddleDancer Press 出版的同名书籍了解更多，也可以通过非暴力沟通中心（Center for Nonviolent Communication）获取其他资源。

Communicate Constantly持续沟通

Constant communication is about staying connected and ensuring a steady flow of information between you, your team, and stakeholders. It's not just about being available; it's about building a culture where sharing, listening, and collab-oration become a regular part of your work.

持续沟通指的是保持连接，并确保你、你的团队和干系人之间有稳定的信息流。它不只是“随叫随到”，更是营造一种文化，让分享、倾听和协作成为你日常工作的常态。

Here's how to make this work in your role:

下面是如何在你的岗位上做到这一点：

  • Hold regular check-ins — One of the most reliable tools for maintaining open lines of communication is recurring one-on-ones. These aren't limited to just your team members. I try to schedule regular check-ins with anyone I collaborate with, whether it's my manager, a stakeholder, or a peer. I'll take the opportunity with anyone who's open to a regular conversation, especially early on, because it's a great way to build rapport and trust.定期做 check-in——保持沟通渠道畅通，最可靠的工具之一就是定期一对一。这不限于你的团队成员。我尽量和所有协作对象都安排定期 check-in，无论是我的经理、某位干系人还是平级同事。只要对方愿意定期聊一聊，我都会抓住这个机会，尤其是在初期，因为这是建立融洽关系和信任的好办法。
  • These one-on-ones serve multiple purposes. They help build trust, catch issues early, and make sure alignment doesn't drift. They also create space for deeper, more honest conversations than what you'll get in a standup or async chat. Think of them as part of your communication hygiene; if you keep them up regularly, everything else tends to flow more smoothly.这些一对一会谈有多重作用。它们帮助建立信任、尽早发现问题，并确保对齐不跑偏。它们还创造了空间，让你能进行比站会或异步聊天更深入、更坦诚的对话。把它们看作你“沟通卫生”的一部分：只要坚持定期做，其他一切往往都会更顺畅。
  • You might be thinking, “But this will take up all my working time.” And yes, it does take time. But this is a big part of your work. Investing early in relationships saves you hours later. When these relationships are already in place, everything from resolving conflicts to asking for support becomes easier. Of course, you don't need to spend your entire week in one-on-ones. The frequency and format should flex based on the context. Your team may need more consistent support, while stakeholders may change or have less availability. The key is to make communication a habit, not just a reaction to problems. Build those bridges early and keep them open.你可能会想：“可这会占满我所有工作时间。”是的，它确实要花时间。但这本来就是你工作的重要组成部分。早期在关系上投资，能帮你日后省下大量时间。当这些关系已经就位，从解决冲突到请求支持，一切都会变得更容易。当然，你不必把整周都耗在一对一里。频率和形式应根据情境灵活调整：你的团队可能需要更持续的支持，而干系人可能会变动、或没那么多时间。关键是让沟通成为一种习惯，而不只是出了问题才反应。早点把桥搭起来，并一直保持畅通。
— PDF p.82 —
  • Communicate progress continuously — Keep everyone, both your team and your stakeholders, in the loop through-out the journey, not just when you've reached a milestone or solved a major problem. Share updates on progress, blockers, mistakes, and changes in direction, about both the good and the uncomfortable.持续沟通进展——让所有人（包括你的团队和干系人）在整个过程中都处于信息环里，而不只是在你达成里程碑或解决了某个大问题时才通知。分享进展、阻塞、失误和方向调整的更新，包括好消息和那些让人不自在的部分。
  • Have a clear, shared way to track progress that's visible and easy to access. Whether it's a roadmap, dashboard, tracking board, or shared doc, it should reflect what's happening and help everyone stay aligned. Even more important than the tool is the habit: make time to review progress together, through weekly check-ins, async updates, or retrospectives.建立一种清晰、共享的进展跟踪方式，让大家都看得见、容易访问。无论是路线图、仪表盘、跟踪看板还是共享文档，它都应如实反映正在发生的事，帮助所有人保持对齐。比工具更重要的是习惯：留出时间一起回顾进展，通过每周 check-in、异步更新或回顾会来做到。
  • Avoid being a knowledge silo — If you're the only one who knows something, it's a problem. You don't want to become a blocker, or worse, the single point of failure. When people rely only on you for a particular topic or piece of information, it creates bottlenecks and slows down the team. It also signals that you may not trust others to take ownership or contribute.不要做知识孤岛——如果某件事只有你知道，那就是个问题。你不会想成为一个阻塞点，更糟的是成为单点故障。当大家在某个主题或某条信息上只能依靠你时，就会形成瓶颈、拖慢团队。这也传递出一个信号：你可能不信任别人能承担责任或做出贡献。
  • Instead, make it a habit to share information proactively with both your team and your stakeholders. Don't keep things to yourself. Whether it's context from a leadership meeting, technical decisions, lessons learned, or simply something you're noticing, bring it into the open. The more you share, the more others can participate, make informed decisions, and act independently. By passing along insights, even small ones, you're showing trust and earning it in return.相反，养成主动向团队和干系人分享信息的习惯。不要把事情攥在自己手里。无论是领导层会议的背景、技术决策、经验教训，还是你注意到的某个现象，都把它摆到台面上。你分享得越多，别人就越能参与、做出有依据的决策并独立行动。通过传递见解——哪怕是很小的见解——你既是在表达信任，也在收获信任。
— PDF p.83 —

Staying connected through constant communication is how trust starts to grow. Showing up regularly, keeping people in the loop, and sharing information openly builds a solid foundation for your relationships.

通过持续沟通保持连接，信任才开始生长。定期出现、让大家身处信息环、公开分享信息，会为你的关系打下坚实的基础。

Be Transparent in Your Communication沟通要透明

Transparency can be complicated for tech leads. Deciding what to share, when, and how much depends heavily on the situation and your team's context.

对技术负责人来说，透明可能很微妙。分享什么、何时分享、分享多少，很大程度上取决于情境和团队的具体情况。

Many tech leads, myself included, fall into the habit of keeping things to themselves. The reasoning often stems from trying to protect the team, not knowing how to frame the information, or simply wanting to maintain control of the narrative. This can extend to stakeholders, where fears of repercussions or “they don't need to know yet” lead to delays in sharing issues, hoping they'll resolve before anyone notices. But the problem is that information flows. When people discover something from someone else, the situation often feels worse than if it had come directly from you. Transparency builds trust; trying to hide things undermines it.

很多技术负责人（包括我自己）都会养成把事情藏在心里的习惯。背后的理由往往是想保护团队、不知道该如何措辞，或者只是想掌控叙事。这种做法也会延伸到干系人身上：出于对后果的担忧，或是“他们现在还不需要知道”，我们迟迟不把问题讲出来，指望它在有人注意到之前自行解决。但问题在于信息是会流动的。当别人从别处得知某事时，局面往往会比当初直接从你这里得知更糟糕。透明建立信任；试图隐瞒则破坏信任。

Breaking out of the habit of withholding information isn't easy, but you can work on it gradually, one step at a time. Here are practical strategies to help you integrate transparency into your daily routine:

打破“ withholding 信息”的习惯并不容易，但你可以一步一步地慢慢改。下面是一些实用策略，帮你把透明融入日常：

  • Be honest about both progress and problems — Transparent communication means that if something prevents progress, you let your team and stakeholders know as early as possible so they can plan accordingly. If something's worrying you, whether it's a risk, a misalignment, or something that just feels off, raise it. Don't wait until it becomes a bigger issue. Addressing things early, together, gives others the chance to contribute and often leads to better decisions.对进展和问题都坦诚——透明的沟通意味着：如果有什么东西阻碍了进展，你要尽早让团队和干系人知道，好让他们相应地做计划。如果有什么让你担心——无论是一个风险、一处对齐偏差，还是单纯感觉不对劲——就把它提出来。别等到它变成更大的问题。及早一起处理，能让别人有机会贡献力量，也往往带来更好的决策。
  • For example, let's say your team underestimated the complexity of integrating with another system, and what initially looked like a small task is now causing delays. Or maybe a risk you flagged earlier has materialized into a real blocker. The moment you realize this will impact timelines, communicate it, even if you don't have all the answers yet. A simple message to stakeholders like “We hit an unexpected issue with the integration that might affect the release date. We're working on a mitigation plan and will update you tomorrow” is far better than delivering bad news late or having people find out from other sources that things aren't going according to plan. Early updates give people the chance to adjust.举个例子：假设你的团队低估了与另一套系统集成的复杂度，原本看着像个小任务，现在却在造成延期。又或者你早先标记过的一个风险，已经变成了真正的阻塞。一旦你意识到这会影响时间线，就讲出来——哪怕你还没有全部答案。给干系人发一条简短消息，比如“集成上遇到一个意料之外的问题，可能影响发布日期。我们正在制定缓解方案，明天给你们更新”，远远好过晚些才宣布坏消息、或者让别人从别处发现事情没按计划走。早期的更新让大家有机会调整。
— PDF p.84 —
  • Provide balanced feedback — Another way to build trust is by giving both positive and improvement feedback. It takes courage to be open about areas for growth, but this balanced approach shows genuine investment in others' development. Offering feedback this way helps people know you're honest with them and truly interested in their growth, not just in keeping things positive. It's the combination of encouragement and constructive insight that reinforces trust and strengthens your relationship.给出平衡的反馈——建立信任的另一种方式，是既给出正面反馈也给出改进反馈。坦诚地指出成长空间需要勇气，但这种平衡的做法表明你真的在意对方的发展。这样给反馈能让对方知道你对他们诚实、真心希望他们成长，而不只是想维持一团和气。正是鼓励与建设性洞察的结合，巩固了信任、加深了你们的关系。
  • Lead with vulnerability — A lot of tech leads go out of their way to hide their mistakes, fearing it might make them seem weak or cause them to lose their team's respect. The truth is, admitting when you don't have all the answers or when you've made a mistake often has the opposite effect: it makes you relatable and authentic. People already know no one is perfect, and acknowledging this builds trust.用脆弱性引领——很多技术负责人千方百计掩盖自己的错误，怕这样会显得软弱、或失去团队的尊重。事实是，承认自己并非无所不知、承认自己犯了错，往往会产生相反的效果：它让你更有人缘、更真实。大家本来就知道没有人是完美的，承认这一点反而能建立信任。
  • For example, if a technical decision you advocated for led to delays or issues, admit it to your team and stakeholders: “This approach didn't work as I hoped, and it's caused these delays. Here's what we've learned, and this is how we're addressing it.” This kind of openness builds stronger connections, creating a culture where your team feels safe to own their mistakes too.举个例子：如果你力主的一个技术决策导致了延期或问题，就向团队和干系人承认：“这个方案没达到我预期的效果，造成了这些延期。这是我们学到的，这是我们正在处理的方式。”这种坦诚能建立更牢固的连接，营造一种文化，让你的团队也敢于为自己的错误负责。

If you find yourself holding back, these strategies can push you out of your comfort zone and help you confront the fear of sharing. Over time, you'll develop new ways to handle interactions and manage challenges directly, instead of stay-ing in the “safe zone” and risking bigger issues. Reflect on your reasons for with-holding information. If it's simply “I'm unsure how my team will react,” share it anyway. The real challenge is learning to navigate their reactions effectively.

如果你发现自己总是有所保留，这些策略能把你推出舒适区，帮你直面“害怕分享”的恐惧。久而久之，你会发展出处理互动、直面挑战的新方式，而不是待在“安全区”里、冒着出更大问题的风险。反思一下你隐瞒信息的理由。如果理由仅仅是“我不确定团队会作何反应”，那还是分享吧。真正的挑战，是学会有效地应对他们的反应。

On the flip side, there's oversharing. Let's say your engineering manager shares news of a potential company restructuring, and you're one of the first to know. You don't yet have concrete details, and a big product launch is two weeks away. If you share this prematurely, you risk creating unnecessary anxiety and distraction, especially since you can't provide clarity or answer questions yet. Sharing too much too soon can harm focus and productivity.

反过来，还有“过度分享”这回事。假设你的工程经理透露公司可能要重组，而你是最早知道的人之一。你还没有具体细节，而一次重要的产品发布就在两周后。如果你过早分享，就可能制造不必要的焦虑和分心——尤其因为你此刻还无法给出清晰的说法、也回答不了问题。分享得太多太早，会损害专注和效率。

There's also a category of information that should never be shared more widely, whether out of respect, to maintain trust, or for legal reasons. This includes personal circumstances, details about layoffs, performance issues, con-fidential feedback shared in one-on-ones, or financial information that not every-one has access to. In extreme cases, mishandling this kind of information can even result in legal consequences.

还有一类信息，无论出于尊重、维护信任还是法律原因，都绝不应广泛传播。这包括个人境遇、裁员细节、绩效问题、在一对一当中分享的保密反馈，以及并非所有人都有权限查看的财务信息。在极端情况下，处理不当这类信息甚至可能招致法律后果。

— PDF p.85 —

So how do you find the balance? Transparency is a judgment call that depends on context. The “right” amount of sharing varies based on timing, audience, and the nature of the information. With time you will learn to read the room and adapt your communication accordingly.

那如何找到平衡呢？透明是一个依情境而定的判断。“恰当”的分享量会因时机、受众和信息性质而异。随着时间推移，你会学会读懂气氛，并相应调整你的沟通。

Start by asking yourself a few key questions:

先问自己几个关键问题：

  • Is it OK to share? — Check with your EM if this is something that can be shared with the team. If not, the decision is clear. If it's up to you, ask for their perspective to help guide your choice.可以分享吗？——和你的工程经理确认这件事是否可以分享给团队。如果不可以，决定就很清楚。如果由你判断，也听听他的看法来辅助你的选择。
  • What additional context do I need? — Gather more details about the timeline and potential impacts from your EM or other tech leads. More information helps you decide what's worth sharing.我还需要哪些背景？——从你的工程经理或其他技术负责人那里，收集关于时间线和潜在影响的更多细节。信息越充分，越有助于你判断什么值得分享。
  • What's the team's maturity level? — Teams with more junior members may react more emotionally to uncertainty, while senior teams might handle ambiguity better. Tailor your approach based on their capacity to process and stay focused.团队的成熟度如何？——初级成员较多的团队，面对不确定性可能情绪反应更强；而资深团队可能更好地应对模糊性。根据他们消化信息、保持专注的能力来调整你的做法。

Neither extreme, keeping information or oversharing, is the answer. Finding the middle ground is about intentional experimentation. Start by recognizing your default tendency. If you lean toward withholding, challenge yourself to share earlier than usual and track what happens. Did the reaction align with your fears, or was it better than expected? Gather feedback and adjust based on the results.

两个极端——把信息捂起来或过度分享——都不是答案。找到中间地带，靠的是有意识地试验。先认清你的默认倾向。如果你倾向于 withholding，就挑战自己比平时更早分享，然后观察发生了什么。对方的反应和你担心的一样吗？还是比预期的好？收集反馈，并根据结果调整。

For me, my instinct has always been to keep things to myself. It felt safer and gave me a sense of control. But over time, I realized that sharing, even when it made me uncomfortable, almost always led to better outcomes. When I was up front about issues or potential delays, my team and stakeholders felt included and trusted me more.

对我来说，我的本能一直是把事情藏在自己心里。那样感觉更安全，也给我一种掌控感。但随着时间推移，我发现：哪怕让我不自在，分享几乎总能带来更好的结果。当我坦率地讲出问题或潜在延期时，我的团队和干系人会感到被包容，也更信任我。

Transparency helps your team align better, work with less confusion, and feel valued. It creates credibility with stakeholders and strengthens relationships across the board.

透明能帮你的团队更好地对齐、在更少困惑下工作，并感到被重视。它在干系人面前建立可信度，并全面加固各种关系。

— PDF p.86 —

Follow Through on Commitments兑现承诺

The simplest way to build trust is to say you'll do something…and then do it.

建立信任最简单的方式，就是说你要做某件事……然后真的去做。

Actions speak louder than words. You can communicate clearly, frequently, and transparently, but if your actions don't align with your words, trust breaks down fast. Follow-through is where trust becomes real.

行动胜于言辞。你可以清晰、频繁、透明地沟通，但如果你的行动与言语不一致，信任会迅速崩塌。说到做到，才让信任变得真实。

People need to see that they can count on you. That means doing what you say you'll do, whether it's shipping a feature, checking in on a topic, or raising a difficult issue with leadership.

大家需要看到他们可以依靠你。这意味着去做你说过要做的事——无论是发布一个特性、跟进某个话题，还是向领导层提出一个棘手的问题。

That might look like agreeing to review a team member's design doc by Friday and actually carving out time by Thursday to leave thoughtful feedback. Or telling your PM that you'll talk to the infrastructure team and then closing the loop a few days later without needing to be chased for updates.

它可能表现为：答应在周五前评审某位团队成员的设计文档，于是真的在周四就腾出时间、留下有思考的反馈；或者告诉产品经理你会去和基础设施团队沟通，然后几天后主动闭环、而不用别人追着要进展。

Even if the task isn't fully done yet, don't wait to communicate. If a team member asks a question in Slack and you said you'd follow up, do it. Even something as simple as “Still looking into this; I haven't forgotten” can go a long way in reinforcing trust.

即便任务还没完全做完，也不要等着才沟通。如果有人在 Slack 里问了个问题、而你说过会跟进，就去跟进。哪怕只是一句“还在查这件事，我没忘”，也能大大巩固信任。

Things won't always go to plan. If something slips, say so early. If you underestimated a task, let people know. A quick message like “I'm still working on this; running behind but I'll share a draft tomorrow,” shows accountability and keeps others from worrying or guessing. And if you drop the ball on a follow-up, acknowledge it. Let people know where things stand and what's next. Silence only creates confusion.

事情不会总按计划走。如果有什么事滑期了，就早点说。如果你低估了某个任务，就告诉大家。一句简短的消息，比如“我还在做这件事，进度落后了，但明天会给大家一版草稿”，既体现担当，也免得别人担心或瞎猜。而如果你把跟进搞砸了，就承认它。让大家知道现在进展到哪、下一步是什么。沉默只会制造困惑。

Follow-through also matters when things are ambiguous or uncomfortable. A team member once asked me for a raise. Being in a startup, we didn't have a formal process, and I knew budget constraints meant it was unlikely to be approved. Still, I promised to raise the topic with the CEO, and I did. The outcome wasn't a yes, but we agreed to revisit the request in six months, which gave the team member clarity and a timeline. Too often, I see people left in limbo on requests like these because it's not an easy conversation. But avoiding hard conversations doesn't make them go away. People should at least know where they stand.

即使事情模糊或令人不快，说到做到同样重要。曾有一位团队成员向我要求加薪。因为是在初创公司，我们没有正式流程；而我也知道预算紧张意味着这事不太可能获批。但我还是答应向 CEO 提出这个话题，并且我做到了。结果不是同意，但我们约定六个月后再重新讨论这个请求，这给了这位成员清晰的答复和时间线。我常常看到，因为这类对话不容易，大家就被晾在一边、悬而未决。但回避艰难对话并不会让它消失。大家至少应该知道自己处于什么位置。

Reliability is built through repetition. It's about showing up consistently, keeping your word, and owning your actions, especially when it's hard. Over time, people start to notice: when you say you'll do something, it gets done. And that kind of reputation becomes one of the most powerful leadership tools you can earn.

可靠是靠重复建立起来的。它在于始终如一的出现、信守承诺、为自己的行为负责——尤其是在困难的时候。久而久之，大家会注意到：当你说要做某件事，它就会被做成。而这样的声誉，会成为你能赢得的最强大的领导力工具之一。

— PDF p.87 —

Who to Build Relationships With该和谁建立关系

As a tech lead, your work doesn't happen in a vacuum. You're not just collaborat-ing with your immediate team but also navigating relationships with your man-ager, cross-functional peers, and a range of stakeholders across the organization. Each of these relationships plays a different role in your success and requires a different approach. In this section, I'll show you how to apply the principles of building strong relationships from the previous section to strengthen these connections.

作为技术负责人，你的工作不是在真空中进行的。你不仅要和自己的直属团队协作，还要经营与经理、跨部门平级同事、以及组织内各类干系人的关系。每一种关系在你的成功中扮演不同角色，也需要不同的打法。本节我会向你展示，如何把上一节讲的建立牢固关系的原则，应用到这些关系上。

Team Members团队成员

These are the people who shape your daily experience. The strength of your bond with your team members directly impacts not only how well you work together but also the quality of your outcomes. Building these relationships requires deliberate effort and consistency beyond occasional conversations.

这些人塑造着你每天的工作体验。你与团队成员之间的纽带有多牢固，不仅直接影响你们协作得好不好，也影响产出的质量。建立这些关系需要有意的投入和持续经营，而不只是偶尔聊聊天。

Here are actionable strategies to build strong relationships within your team:

下面是一些可落地的策略，帮你在团队内部建立牢固关系：

  • Set up one-on-ones — One-on-ones are especially important with your team. One of my first moves when joining a new team is to set up recurring one-on-ones with each team member. The frequency might adjust, or we might skip one occasionally, but the important part is that they're in the calendar. Just having that space booked gives your team confidence that you're there, that you're invested, and that you'll continue to show up.安排一对一——一对一和团队成员尤其重要。我加入新团队后最先做的事之一，就是和每位成员安排定期一对一会谈。频率可能调整，偶尔也可能跳过一次，但重要的是它们已经写进日历。仅仅把那个时间块预定下来，就能让团队确信：你在、你投入、你会持续出现。
  • These meetings are so much more than status updates. In fact, updates should be just a small part of them. One-on-ones are your best chance to notice when someone's struggling, whether with workload, motivation, or something personal. They create a space where people feel safe to be honest. If someone is underperforming or going through a tough patch, this is the time to dig deeper, offer support, and align on a way forward. If you want to dive deeper into how to approach these conversations with your team, check out Chapter 4. It covers everything from setting them up to dealing with common challenges, like when someone shuts down or you're unsure how to help.这些会谈远不止进展同步。事实上，进展更新只应占其中很小一部分。一对一你最好的机会去发现某人正处于困境——无论是工作量、动力还是个人方面的事。它们创造了一个让大家敢于坦诚的空间。如果有人表现不佳或正经历一段艰难时期，这就是深入了解、提供支持、并就前进方向达成一致的时机。如果你想更深入地学习如何与团队进行这类对话，请看第 4 章。它涵盖了从如何安排会谈，到应对常见挑战的方方面面——比如有人沉默不语、或你不知道该怎么帮忙。
— PDF p.88 —
  • Make feedback routine — Treat feedback as a natural and regular part of daily interactions rather than a formal event. Consistently sharing both positive and constructive feedback builds trust and shows your genuine commitment to your team's development. Addressing areas for improvement may require courage, but combining encouragement with actionable insights makes team members feel supported and motivated to improve. Encouraging your team to exchange feedback among themselves amplifies this effect, strengthening connections and collaboration across the group. If you want to go deeper into how to ask for, give, and create a healthy feedback culture in your team, check out Chapter 5. It covers everything from the five principles of good feedback to the practicalities of making it work day-to-day, including the most common challenges tech leads face and how to overcome them.让反馈成为常态——把反馈当作日常互动中自然而常规的一部分，而不是一场正式活动。持续分享正面和建设性反馈，能建立信任，并表明你真心在意团队的成长。指出改进空间可能需要勇气，但把鼓励与可落地的洞见结合起来，会让团队成员感到被支持、并有动力改进。鼓励团队成员彼此交换反馈，会放大这种效果，加强整个群体的连接与协作。如果你想更深入地学习如何请求反馈、给出反馈、并在团队中营造健康的反馈文化，请看第 5 章。它涵盖了良好反馈的五条原则，以及让反馈在日常运转起来的实操细节，包括技术负责人最常遇到的挑战及应对方法。
  • Say “I don't know” more often — A simple and effective way to connect with your team and build trust is to show that you don't have all the answers, and that's OK. Saying something as simple as “I don't know” can be a game-changer. It removes the pressure to pretend, accelerates your learning because you're more likely to seek answers, and creates a safer space for others to admit when they're unsure too. Using phrases like “I don't know, but I'll find out” or “Let's figure it out together” not only shows humility but also strengthens your credibility.更常说“我不知道”——与团队连接、建立信任，一个简单而有效的办法是表明你并非无所不知，而这没关系。说出一句简单的“我不知道”，可能成为一个转折点。它卸下了你假装全知的压力，加速了你的学习（因为你会更主动去寻找答案），也为别人创造了一个更安全的空间，让他们在不确定时也敢于承认。用“我不知道，但我会去查清楚”或“我们一起来弄明白吧”这样的说法，不仅展现谦逊，还增强你的可信度。
  • Give your team more autonomy — Fear of losing control is common for tech leads, often leading them to micromanage: tracking everyone's progress, constantly checking in, or reacting negatively when things don't go as planned. This behavior creates discomfort and causes team members to avoid you, harming your relationship with them. Strike a balance between being available and overbearing. Be approachable for questions and problems, but also give your team the space to work independently, make mistakes, and learn without fear of your reaction. The right amount of independence and guidance isn't one-size-fits-all. More junior team members might need more structure and might reach out more often, while senior engineers often thrive with greater flexibility. Tailor your level of involvement based on the individual or team's experience and confidence.给团队更多自主权——害怕失控是技术负责人的通病，常常导致微观管理：追踪每个人的进度、不停地 check-in、或在事情不如预期时反应负面。这种行为让人不适，会让团队成员躲着你，损害你们的关系。在“随时在场”和“咄咄逼人”之间找到平衡：既让人方便找你问问题、求助，也给团队独立工作、犯错、学习的空间，而不必害怕你的反应。自主权与指导的恰当分寸并非一刀切。初级成员可能需要更多结构、也更常来求助；而资深工程师往往在更大的灵活性下表现更好。根据个人或团队的经验与信心，调整你介入的程度。
— PDF p.89 —
  • A powerful way to build autonomy is through delegation. Identify a task (you can get ideas in Chapter 6), select the right person, and set clear expectations. Offer support but then step aside. This shows your team you trust their skills: “I trust you to take care of this.” When team members feel trusted, they're more likely to trust you, strengthening your relationship. Plus, prioritizing their growth shows you value their development, which they'll deeply appreciate, building even stronger connections.建立自主权的一个有力方式是授权。找出一个任务（你可以在第 6 章获得灵感）、选对人、设定清晰的期望。提供支持，然后退到一边。这向团队表明你信任他们的能力：“我相信你能把这件事处理好。”当团队成员感到被信任，他们也更可能信任你，从而加固你们的关系。此外，把他们的成长放在优先位置，表明你看重他们的发展——他们会深为感激，进而建立更牢固的连接。
  • Focus on solutions, not blame — When things go wrong, don't make it about pointing fingers; focus on fixing the problem. A team that knows they won't be blamed for mistakes will feel safer to share challenges and work together to solve them. Mistakes are inevitable, but how you handle them can either strengthen or break your team. Take a production incident as an example. If your response is “Whose fault is this?” you're setting a tone of fear and mistrust. People will start hiding their mistakes, avoiding accountability, and holding back potential issues because they're afraid of how you'll react. But if you shift the focus to “How can we solve this?” or “What ideas do you have to fix this?” you send a different message: mistakes happen, and that's OK, as long as we learn from them and tackle them together. Handling things this way creates opportunities for your team to bond. There's no better team-building exercise than solving a tough problem together. By consistently approaching issues with a solutions mindset, you'll build a culture of shared responsibility, where the whole team feels accountable for both successes and failures. Over time, your team will follow your lead and stop looking for someone to blame, focusing instead on how to move forward together.关注解决方案，而不是指责——出了问题，不要把精力放在指责任何人身上；专注于解决问题。一个知道犯错不会被指责的团队，会更敢于分享困难、并一起协作解决它们。错误不可避免，但你如何处理它们，既能加固也能打散你的团队。以一次生产事故为例。如果你的反应是“这是谁的锅？”，你就在设定一种恐惧和不信任的基调。大家会开始隐藏错误、逃避责任、并隐瞒潜在问题，因为他们害怕你的反应。但如果你把焦点转到“我们怎么解决这个问题？”或“你有什么修复的主意？”，你传递的就是另一种信息：错误会发生，这没关系，只要我们从中学习、一起应对。这样处理事情，为团队创造了建立感情的机会。没有什么比一起解决一个难题更好的团队建设活动了。始终以解决问题的心态面对问题，你就会建立一种共担责任的文化，让整个团队为成功和失败共同负责。久而久之，你的团队会效仿你，不再找人背锅，而是专注于如何一起向前走。
Note. How you lead when things go wrong says a lot about you as a tech lead. Those moments show your true character, and they're where trust is built, or lost. Choose wisely.注意。出问题时你如何引领，很能说明你作为技术负责人的成色。那些时刻会展现你真正的品格，也是信任被建立、或被毁掉的地方。请明智地选择。

These strategies, when applied consistently, will strengthen the connections within your team, creating an environment built on trust, collaboration, and con-tinuous growth. With these relationships in place, your team will feel supported, empowered, and equipped to deliver better results.

这些策略若能坚持应用，会加固团队内部的连接，营造一个建立在信任、协作和持续成长之上的环境。有了这些关系，你的团队会感到被支持、被赋能，并具备交付更好成果的能力。

— PDF p.90 —

Managers经理们

Your first team stakeholders are your managers, and they can either help you or be a real roadblock; it usually depends on your relationship with them, not just on having good arguments. When you've already established a connection, your suggestions and decisions tend to land better:

你的第一批团队干系人就是你的经理们，他们既可以帮你，也可能成为真正的障碍；而这通常取决于你和他们的关系，而不仅仅是你论据是否充分。当你们已经建立起连接，你的建议和决策往往更容易被接受：

  • Make one-on-ones a priority — If your manager or stakeholders don't initiate one-on-ones, take the lead and set them up yourself. These meetings don't need to be as frequent as the ones with your team; every two weeks or even monthly can work, depending on the stakeholder. The important part is consistency. Show up prepared and organized to make their job easier. Bring notes, ask thoughtful questions, and show genuine interest in their work. Often, tech leads hesitate to request these meetings, assuming stakeholders have more important things to do, but the truth is they also benefit from these conversations. One-on-ones are an opportunity to address potential issues early, align on priorities, and gain valuable insight into broader organizational goals. If they're too busy, they can decline. All you have to do is ask.把一对一放在优先位置——如果你的经理或干系人不主动发起一对一，你就带头自己去约。这些会议不必像和团队那样频繁；每两周甚至每月一次都可以，取决于干系人。重要的是保持一致。带着准备和条理出现，让他们的工作更轻松。带上笔记、提出有思考的问题、并对他们的工作表现出真诚的兴趣。技术负责人常常犹豫要不要约这种会，以为干系人有更重要的事要做，但事实是他们也能从这些对话中受益。一对一是一个及早处理潜在问题、对齐优先级、并更深入了解组织大目标的机会。如果他们太忙，可以婉拒。你只需要开口问。
  • Highlight your team's work — For all the effort your team puts into their work, you should match that by finding ways to make it visible to stakeholders. A great starting point is investing in showcases. These are presentations where your team shares what they've been working on, like new features, progress, or key learnings, with others outside the team, especially stakeholders. They're a chance to keep everyone in the loop and show the impact of your collective work. Treat them like value-delivering tasks, not just routine meetings. Add them to your team board, set time aside to define what you want to highlight, prepare the presentation thoroughly, and rehearse your delivery. When done right, showcases can bring tremendous visibility to your team's work and trust from stakeholders. For example, my team's well-prepared showcases made us the first choice when a high-profile product opportunity appeared.突出你团队的工作——你的团队在工作上付出了那么多努力，你也应当相应地想办法让它在干系人面前被看见。一个很好的起点是投入做展示会（showcase）。这是一种汇报形式，让团队向团队之外的人（尤其是干系人）分享他们一直在做的事——比如新特性、进展或关键经验教训。它们是让大家身处信息环、并展示你们集体工作影响力的机会。把它们当成“交付价值的任务”来对待，而不只是例行会议。把它们加进团队看板、留出时间明确你想突出什么、彻底准备演示内容，并排练你的表达。做得好的话，展示会能为团队的工作带来巨大的可见度，并赢得干系人的信任。例如，我团队精心准备的展示会，让我们在一个高关注度产品机会出现时成为首选。
— PDF p.91 —
  • The key to building trust during these showcases is transparency. Don't just celebrate wins but also share the challenges your team faced and the lessons learned. This openness reassures stakeholders that they can trust you to deliver while being honest about what didn't work. Ending with a feedback session is a cherry on top, encouraging conversation and engaging stakeholders who might not otherwise get involved. This process doesn't rest solely on you. Rotate team members to lead showcases; it gives them visibility, strengthens their skills, and boosts their pride in the work. Outside of showcases, one-on-ones with stakeholders can also be an opportunity to share team successes, as well as to build personal connections. Even something as simple as sharing progress updates in public Slack channels can make a difference; you never know who might notice.在这些展示会中建立信任的关键是透明。不要只庆祝胜利，也要分享团队遇到的挑战和学到的教训。这种坦诚让干系人放心：他们可以信任你交付，同时你也会诚实地讲出哪些没成。以一场反馈环节收尾，更是锦上添花，能鼓励对话、让那些原本可能不参与的干系人也加入进来。这个过程不必全压在你身上。轮流让团队成员来主持展示会；这能让他们获得可见度、锻炼技能、并增强对工作的自豪感。在展示会之外，与干系人的一对一也可以成为分享团队成功、并建立个人连接的机会。哪怕只是在公开的 Slack 频道里分享进展更新，也能带来不同——你永远不知道谁会注意到。
  • Ask for mentorship — One of the easiest ways to build new relationships, especially with people you don't interact with daily, is to ask for mentorship. It doesn't have to be formal or long term. A simple request like “I've noticed how well you handle stakeholder conversations. I'd love to learn more about your approach. Would you be open to a quick chat sometime?” can open the door to a deeper connection. People generally appreciate being asked for advice or perspective, especially when it's specific and genuine. It shows that you respect their experience and want to learn from them, and that builds trust fast. Sometimes, what starts as a one-off chat grows into a longer-term mentorship relationship. You may find yourself checking in regularly, exchanging updates, or turning to them during tough moments, without ever needing to label it as formal mentorship. Just like any strong relationship, it develops naturally over time.请求指导——建立新关系（尤其是与你日常不打交道的人）最简单的方式之一，就是请求对方指点。它不必正式，也不必长期。一句简单的请求，比如“我注意到你处理与干系人的对话特别出色，我很想多学学你的方法。方便找时间简单聊聊吗？”，就能为更深入的连接打开大门。人们通常乐于被征求建议或看法，尤其是当请求具体而真诚时。这表明你尊重他们的经验、想向他们学习，而这能快速建立信任。有时，一次偶然的聊天会发展成长期的指导关系。你可能会发现自己开始定期 check-in、交换进展、或在艰难时刻求助于他们，而从不需要把它定义成正式的导师关系。和任何牢固关系一样，它会随时间自然发展。
— PDF p.92 —
  • Managers are a great starting point, even if they're not in your direct reporting line. They often bring a broader organizational view and can help you see how your role fits into the bigger picture. But don't overlook experienced ICs either; they can share incredibly useful tips on how to lead without official authority or how to handle tricky team dynamics. The key is the conversation. Reaching out like this creates new allies across the organization and builds relationships that may benefit you (and them) in unexpected ways later on.经理们是很好的起点，哪怕他们不在你的直接汇报线上。他们往往带来更宏观的组织视角，能帮你看清你的岗位如何嵌入大局。但也不要忽视有经验的个人贡献者（IC）；他们能分享极其实用的技巧——如何在没有正式职权的情况下引领、如何处理棘手的团队动态。关键在于那场对话。像这样主动接触，会在组织内结交新的盟友，并建立起日后可能以意想不到的方式让你（和他们）受益的关系。
  • Show up at events and use casual moments to build connections — All-hands meetings, leadership events, or casual gatherings like coffee breaks and holiday parties are perfect chances to connect with stakeholders and managers. Even if you find these events boring, they're a great way to build relationships. A quick comment like “I really enjoyed your talk on [topic]” can leave a positive impression and make follow-ups easier. If a manager offers an informal coffee chat or an “Ask me anything” session, jump on it. Showing up, even when others shy away, sets you apart and opens doors for more meaningful conversations.出席活动、利用非正式时刻建立连接——全员大会、领导层活动，或是茶歇、节日聚会这类非正式场合，都是与干系人和经理建立连接的绝佳机会。哪怕你觉得这些活动无聊，它们也是建立关系的好办法。一句简短的评论，比如“我很喜欢你关于［某主题］的分享”，就能留下正面印象，让后续跟进更容易。如果某位经理提供非正式咖啡聊天或“随便问我”环节，就抓住它。即使别人都回避，你依然出现，这会让你与众不同，并为更有意义的对话打开大门。

By investing in these relationships, you'll find that managers are more likely to support your initiatives, making things smoother for both you and your team.

通过投资这些关系，你会发现经理们更愿意支持你的项目，从而让你和团队的日子都更顺畅。

Other Stakeholders其他干系人

Your team doesn't work in isolation; every move you make will impact other teams and roles: product managers, designers, cross-functional departments like sales, finance, legal, customer service, and, of course, your users or clients (if applicable). These stakeholders also influence your work and can directly affect how effectively your team achieves its goals.

你的团队不是孤立工作的；你的每一个动作都会影响其他团队和角色：产品经理、设计师、销售、财务、法务、客服等跨职能部门，当然还有你的用户或客户（如果适用的话）。这些干系人也会影响你的工作，并能直接影响你团队达成目标的效率。

Here are a few ways to make these connections work for you and your team:

下面是一些办法，让这些连接为你和你的团队发挥作用：

  • Open cross-team communication channels — Let's take a common example: your team depends on another team to deliver part of a project. Their progress directly impacts your timeline, and vice versa. The easiest way to ensure smooth communication is by setting up a dedicated Slack channel or space for both teams. This becomes a central hub for updates, questions, and discussions. Recurring check-ins are another great way to keep everyone aligned. These don't need to be long or formal, just a quick sync to share progress and address potential blockers. Of course, you don't have to manage this relationship alone. You can pair up with someone from your team who has an interest in the topic or assign them to take ownership of the communication. This not only keeps updates flowing smoothly but also gives your team a chance to build relationships with the other team, a win for everyone involved.打通跨团队沟通渠道——举个常见例子：你的团队依赖另一个团队交付项目的一部分。他们的进度直接影响你的时间线，反之亦然。确保沟通顺畅最简单的办法，就是为两个团队建立一个专门的 Slack 频道或空间。它会成为更新、提问和讨论的中心枢纽。定期 check-in 是让大家保持对齐的另一个好办法。不必很长或很正式，只需快速同步一下进展、处理潜在阻塞。当然，你不必独自管理这段关系。你可以在团队里找一个对这个主题感兴趣的人搭档，或让他来负责沟通。这不仅让更新顺畅流转，也让你的团队有机会与对方团队建立关系——对所有人都是双赢。
— PDF p.93 —
  • Ask for help, and offer it — Asking for help is one of the easiest and most underused strategies to build relationships. Instead of wasting days stuck on a problem, tap into the collective knowledge of your organization. Post questions in general or team-specific Slack channels like “Has anyone worked on this before?” or “Can someone help with this?” You'd be surprised how often people are willing to assist. Similarly, take the initiative to help others. Answer unanswered questions in Slack or reach out to teams facing challenges you've already solved.主动求助，也主动帮人——求助是最简单、却最被低估的建立关系策略之一。与其在一个问题上卡好几天，不如调动组织的集体知识。在公开的或团队的 Slack 频道里发帖提问，比如“有人以前做过这个吗？”或“谁能帮我看看这个？”你会惊讶于人们有多么愿意帮忙。同样，主动帮助别人。去回答 Slack 里没人回应的问题，或者主动联系那些正面临你已经解决过的挑战的团队。
  • Build cross-team collaboration spaces — Host monthly tech lead chats: set up recurring sessions where tech leads from different teams come together to share updates, troubleshoot challenges, and brainstorm ideas. To make the most of these sessions, consider assigning a rotating facilitator and preparing a lightweight agenda in advance. This helps keep the conversation focused while still leaving room for organic discussion and peer learning.打造跨团队协作空间——每月主办技术负责人茶话会：安排定期的场次，让来自不同团队的技术负责人聚在一起分享进展、共同排查难题、并头脑风暴。为了让这些场次更有成效，可以考虑轮换主持人，并提前准备一份轻量议程。这能让对话保持聚焦，同时仍为自发讨论和同伴学习留出空间。
  • Create company guilds: establish groups around topics like architecture, frontend development, or cloud migration. Open these guilds to anyone interested, whether engineers, architects, or other stakeholders, to encourage knowledge sharing, alignment, and innovation across teams.建立公司级技术社区（guild）：围绕架构、前端开发、云迁移等主题成立小组。向所有感兴趣的人开放——无论是工程师、架构师还是其他干系人——以鼓励跨团队的知识分享、对齐和创新。
  • Virtual coffee chats (often facilitated by Slack apps like Donut, Alfy, or similar) are an underrated way to connect with colleagues across your organization. While many companies offer these, few people take full advantage of the opportunity. Yet, I've never met a developer who participated and regretted it. These informal chats can spark unexpected connections, open doors to collaboration, and help you build a network that might come in handy when you least expect it. You never know when the person you chat with could be the key to solving a future challenge or opportunity.虚拟咖啡聊天（通常由 Donut、Alfy 之类的 Slack 应用撮合）是一种被低估的、与全公司同事建立连接的方式。虽然很多公司都提供这种机制，却很少有人充分利用这个机会。然而，我从没见过哪位参与过的开发人员后悔。这些非正式的聊天能擦出意料之外的连接火花、打开协作的大门，并帮你建立一张人脉网——它可能在你最意想不到的时候派上用场。你永远不知道，和你聊天的那个人，会不会成为未来某个挑战或机会的关键。
  • Support other teams' initiatives: encourage your team to participate in hackathons, brainstorming sessions, or workshops led by other teams. You can also show up to their demos, give feedback on deliverables, comment on RFCs, or contribute ideas in shared documents and discussions.支持其他团队的项目：鼓励你的团队参加其他团队主办的黑客马拉松、头脑风暴或工作坊。你也可以去看他们的演示、对交付物给出反馈、在 RFC 上评论，或在共享文档和讨论中贡献想法。
  • Invite diverse perspectives to brainstorming — For product kick-offs or major planning sessions, bring in voices from other departments like customer service, sales, or marketing. Instead of only the PM talking to them separately, I've found it more effective to bring everyone together for their take on potential product challenges and solutions up front. Their perspectives often surface challenges and opportunities the core team might miss. Just ask! They can always say no, but the payoff can be significant when they say yes.邀请多元视角参与头脑风暴——在产品启动会或大型规划会议上，把客服、销售、市场等其他部门的声音请进来。与其只让产品经理分别和他们谈，我发现更有效的做法是把大家聚到一起，提前听取他们对潜在产品挑战和方案的看法。他们的视角往往能浮出核心团队可能错过的挑战和机会。开口邀请就好！他们总可以拒绝，但一旦答应，回报可能相当可观。
— PDF p.94 —

These strategies can help you start building connections with your team and different types of stakeholders.

这些策略能帮你着手与团队以及各类干系人建立连接。

Common Challenges and How to Overcome Them常见挑战及应对方法

Building relationships comes with its fair share of challenges, especially as a tech lead. The three most common ones I see tech leads face are breaking the ice with new connections, maintaining strong relationships over time, and effectively bridging the gap with nontechnical stakeholders.

经营关系本身就伴随着不少挑战，对技术负责人尤其如此。我看到技术负责人最常面对的三个挑战是：与新关系破冰、长期维持牢固关系，以及有效地弥合与非技术干系人之间的鸿沟。

For some, these conversations feel easy and natural. They enjoy small talk and are quick to build rapport. But for many others, starting and sustaining these kinds of interactions can feel awkward, mentally draining, or just unclear. Whatever the reason, know that you're not alone and that this is something you can absolutely get better at through practice.

对有些人来说，这些对话轻松而自然。他们喜欢寒暄，能很快建立融洽关系。但对另许多人来说，开启和维持这类互动可能让人尴尬、精神耗竭，或完全不知道该怎么做。无论原因是什么，请知道你不是一个人，而这件事你绝对可以通过练习变得更好。

In this section, I'll dive into the three most common relationship-building challenges mentioned previously and share actionable strategies to help you navigate and overcome them.

本节我会深入讲讲前面提到的三个最常见的经营关系挑战，并分享可落地的策略，帮你应对和克服它们。

It Feels Awkward to Start Conversations开口搭话让人尴尬

Breaking the ice can feel daunting, but without that initial moment of connec-tion, relationships can't begin. Many tech leads overthink the first step: “What should I say? How do I start?” Instead of waiting for opportunities to come to you, take the initiative.

破冰可能让人望而生畏，但没有那最初一刻的连接，关系就无从开始。很多技术负责人把第一步想得太复杂：“我该说什么？怎么开口？”与其等机会找上门，不如主动出击。

A presentation is one of the easiest ways to start a conversation. Speakers expect interaction, so after their talk, show appreciation and highlight a specific point you liked: “I really enjoyed your take on…” Asking a thoughtful question about their content can make the interaction more meaningful, and they'll remember your genuine interest.

一场分享会是开启对话最简单的方式之一。讲者本就期待互动，所以在他们讲完后，表达感谢并点出一个你喜欢的具体观点：“我很喜欢你关于……的看法。”就他们的内容提一个有思考的问题，能让这次互动更有意义，他们也会记住你真诚的兴趣。

If you're working on a shared project, use that as common ground. Reaching out with “I heard you're tackling a similar challenge; how did you approach it?” opens doors naturally.

如果你正在做一个共同的项目，就把它作为共同话题。主动开口说“我听说你也在应对类似的挑战，你是怎么处理的？”，会自然地打开大门。

Similarly, asking for help is an underrated strategy. Most people love sharing their expertise. Be specific: instead of a vague “hello,” start with “I heard you're the go-to for this issue. Can you help?” This clarity increases the chances of a response.

同样，求助是一个被低估的策略。大多数人喜欢分享自己的专长。要具体：不要用一句含糊的“你好”开头，而用“我听说你是这个问题的专家，能帮帮我吗？”开始。这种明确性能提高得到回应的概率。

Don't underestimate the power of active listening. When someone responds, be fully present: pay attention to their words, tone, and body language. Reflecting back what you heard or asking clarifying questions (“So, do you mean…?”) shows that you're not just waiting to speak but are truly engaged. Instead of jumping to your next point, you can use what the other person just said to carry the conversation forward. People are far more likely to remember someone who made them feel heard than someone who had the perfect opening line.

不要低估积极倾听的力量。当对方回应时，全然在场：注意他们的用词、语调和肢体语言。复述你听到的内容，或提出澄清式问题（“所以，你的意思是……？”），表明你不只是在等着开口，而是真正投入其中。不要急着跳到你的下一个论点，而要利用对方刚说的话把对话继续下去。比起那个有完美开场白的人，人们远更容易记住那个让他们感到被倾听的人。

— PDF p.95 —

Also, don't miss opportunities to help others. Answer Slack questions no one has addressed, tag someone who might know, or offer your insight. People notice this effort.

此外，不要错过帮助别人的机会。去回答 Slack 里没人处理的问题、@一下可能知道答案的人，或贡献你的见解。人们会注意到这份用心。

Finally, create spaces where others can approach you (one of my favorites). Host showcases, lead meetings, or run Q&A sessions. It's an easy way to start building connections without having to reach out yourself, as you're creating a space where they can approach you.

最后，创造让别人能主动接近你的空间（这是我个人最偏爱的方式之一）。主办展示会、主持会议、或开问答环节。这是一种轻松建立连接的方式——你不必主动去找别人，因为你创造了一个让他们能接近你的空间。

The more intentional effort you put into breaking the ice, the easier it becomes, and more and more ideas will come up.

你在破冰上投入的有意努力越多，它就越容易，也会有越来越多的点子冒出来。

How Do I Keep Relationships Strong Over Time?如何让关系长期保鲜？

Building relationships is only the first step; maintaining them requires consis-tent effort. Over time, people's priorities shift, and so does the context of your interactions. To keep relationships strong and meaningful, you need to stay intentional and adaptable.

建立关系只是第一步；维护它们需要持续的努力。随着时间推移，人们的优先事项会变，你们互动的情境也会变。要让关系牢固而有意义，你需要保持有意和灵活。

Here are actionable strategies for nurturing these connections over time:

下面是一些可落地的策略，用于长期滋养这些连接：

  • Keep track of people — Make it a habit to jot down memorable details from conversations right after, such as personal interests or key points they've shared. Whether it's a note about their favorite hobby, a challenge they mentioned, or a skill they want to improve, referencing these details in future conversations shows that you care and strengthens the connection.记住关于人的细节——养成习惯，在聊完之后立刻记下对话中值得记住的细节，比如个人兴趣或他们分享过的要点。无论是关于他们最喜欢的爱好、提到的一个挑战，还是想提升的一项技能，在未来对话中引用这些细节，都表明你在意对方，并加固连接。
  • Follow up — When someone helps you, take the time to circle back and share the results. This shows appreciation and keeps the connection alive. Even small updates matter. For example, you could say, “Thanks again for the tip on [topic]. I tried it, and here's what happened: [result].” If someone asks you a question you couldn't answer right away or you left a conversation open-ended, always follow up. Even if it's just to say, “I'm still working on this” or “I couldn't find an answer,” it shows reliability and keeps the dialogue flowing.跟进——当有人帮了你，花时间回头分享结果。这表达了感谢，也让连接保持活跃。哪怕很小的更新也有意义。比如你可以说：“再次谢谢你关于［某主题］的建议。我试了，结果是这样的：［结果］。”如果有人问了你一个你当时答不上来的问题，或者你们的对话没聊完，一定要跟进。哪怕只是一句“我还在处理这件事”或“我没找到答案”，也体现了可靠，并让对话继续流动。
— PDF p.96 —
  • Create recurring touchpoints — Consistency is everything when it comes to maintaining relationships. Avoid skipping one-on-ones with your team or stakeholders, even if it feels like there's nothing urgent to discuss. These moments aren't just about updates; they're about building rapport and staying connected. Make it easy for others by coming prepared: bring updates, questions, or potential issues, and leave space for them to share their own thoughts.创造定期触点——维护关系时，一致性就是一切。不要跳过与团队或干系人的一对一，哪怕感觉没什么急事要谈。这些时刻不只是为了更新；它们是为了建立融洽、保持连接。通过有准备地出现，让别人更容易和你交流：带上进展、问题或潜在议题，也留出空间让他们分享自己的想法。
  • Prioritize and choose battles wisely — Not every relationship requires the same level of attention. For instance, if you're collaborating with another team to deliver a critical feature, it makes sense to focus on building a strong connection with that team and the stakeholders impacted by the feature. Meanwhile, relationships that aren't immediately relevant can temporarily take a backseat. Regularly reassess your priorities as projects and goals shift to ensure your energy is directed where it matters most. Similarly, not every disagreement is worth pursuing. Focus on common ground rather than being right. For example, agreeing with your product manager to move retrospectives from Friday to Monday, even if it's always been Friday, is less impactful than advocating for prioritizing a crucial technical-debt task that could directly affect your product's quality.排定优先级、明智地选择“战役”——并非每段关系都需要同等程度的关注。比如，如果你正和另一个团队协作交付一个关键特性，那么专注于与那个团队以及受该特性影响的干系人建立牢固连接就是合理的。与此同时，暂时不相关的关系可以先放一放。随着项目和目标变化，定期重新评估你的优先级，确保精力投在最重要的地方。同样，并非每一次分歧都值得争到底。关注共同点，而不是争个对错。比如，同意产品经理把回顾会从周五改到周一（哪怕一直都是周五），其影响也不如去主张优先处理一个关键技术债任务——后者可能直接影响产品质量。

Relationships are like living things: they thrive with care and effort but can endure beyond immediate interactions. Once trust and reliability are established, they become self-sustaining. For example, if you've built a strong connection with a stakeholder during a project and reconnect months later, that trust still holds, and you can pick up where you left off. This was clear to me when I transitioned to being self-employed (a solopreneur): past clients, coworkers, and managers reached out with opportunities years later.

关系就像有生命的东西：它们因关爱和努力而茁壮成长，但也能超越眼前的互动而持久。一旦信任和可靠建立起来，它们就能自我维系。比如，如果你在一个项目中与某位干系人建立了牢固连接，几个月后再联系，那份信任依然在，你们可以从上次停下的地方继续。我转型做自由职业（独立创业者）时，这一点体会很深：多年以后，过去的客户、同事和经理还带着各种机会来找我。

Investing in lasting relationships also contributes to building a foundation for your long-term career: there is a high chance you will run into the same people in the future.

投资于持久的关系，也在为你长期的职业发展打基础：你未来很大概率还会遇到同样这些人。

We Just Don't Speak the Same Language我们好像说不到一块儿去

Usually, this means struggling to get on the same page, like you're both talking but not fully understanding each other's perspective. Often, it's because they're deep in business lingo while you're explaining things technically.

通常，这指的是你们难以达成共识——好像双方都在说，却没有真正理解对方的视角。往往是因为他们满口业务术语，而你在用技术语言解释事情。

— PDF p.97 —

Here's how to bridge that gap:

下面是如何弥合这道鸿沟：

  • Step into their world — Start by mentioning how important it is for you to figure this out together and why. This will set the ground for conversation, showing them that you are not going for a fight. Learn what they care about. Everyone's viewpoint comes from their role's priorities, so start by understanding what drives their decisions. Instead of trying to prove to the other person you are right, start by deep diving into their reasoning and arguments. One strategy that I use in these cases is to assume the other person has a valid point, even if I don't fully see it yet. I try to understand their reasoning deeply, believing there's something valuable I might be missing.走进他们的世界——一开始就说明，为什么你认为把这件事一起弄清楚很重要。这会为对话奠定基础，向他们表明你不是来吵架的。去了解他们在意什么。每个人的观点都来自其岗位的优先级，所以先去理解是什么在驱动他们的决策。不要急着向对方证明你是对的，而是先深入挖掘他们的推理和论据。在这种情况下我常用的一个策略是：假设对方有道理，哪怕我还没完全看出来。我努力深入理解他们的推理，相信自己可能遗漏了某些有价值的东西。
  • Ask clarifying questions — Don't assume their intentions or goals. Ask “What's the main priority here?” or “What's the outcome you're aiming for?” Reflect back their answers: “So if I understand correctly, you mean…?” This one simple question can make a huge difference. It may sound small, but repeating back my understanding has helped me avoid countless misunderstandings. Often, the reply is “No, that's not what I meant,” revealing that we weren't actually aligned at all. Most problems in tech teams come from everyone assuming they're already on the same page when they're not.提出澄清式问题——不要臆测他们的意图或目标。问“这里最主要的优先级是什么？”或“你想要达成的结果是什么？”把他们的回答复述出来：“所以如果我没理解错，你的意思是……？”这个简单的问题能带来巨大的不同。它听上去很小，但复述我的理解帮我避免了无数次误解。对方常常会回答“不，我不是那个意思”——这揭示出我们其实根本没对齐。技术团队里的大多数问题，都源于大家以为已经达成共识、其实并没有。
  • Find shared goals — Once you understand their goals, look for common ground. For example, if they're focused on deadlines and you're focused on code quality, point out how both efforts contribute to a successful product launch. Shared goals help align your efforts.找到共同目标——一旦理解了他们的目标，就寻找共同点。比如，如果他们关注交付期限、而你关注代码质量，就指出这两方面的努力如何共同促成一次成功的产品发布。共同目标有助于对齐你们的努力。
  • Use their language — Explain your points in terms that resonate with their priorities. Instead of saying, “We need to refactor,” frame it as “This will reduce risks and save time later.” Adapting your language shows effort to meet them halfway, making your ideas more relatable.用他们的语言——用与他们的优先级产生共鸣的说法来解释你的观点。不要说“我们需要重构”，而要说“这样做会降低风险、并在以后节省时间”。调整你的措辞，展现出你愿意主动靠近对方，让你的想法更容易被接受。

Building a shared language doesn't happen overnight, especially when you're coming from different domains. But with curiosity, patience, and a genuine effort to understand the other person's perspective, it becomes much easier to bridge the gap. Remember: it's not about winning an argument; it's about building alignment and trust. And that starts with showing that you're willing to meet people where they are.

建立共同的语言不是一蹴而就的，尤其当你们来自不同领域时。但带着好奇、耐心，以及真诚去理解对方视角的努力，弥合鸿沟会变得容易得多。请记住：重点不是赢得一场争论，而是建立对齐和信任。而这始于表明你愿意走到对方所在的位置去见他们。

— PDF p.98 —

Building Relationships as an Introvert内向者如何经营关系

Not everyone finds it easy to strike up conversations or navigate social dynamics, especially if you're more introverted. The expectation that tech leads should be constantly engaging can feel overwhelming when your natural preference is for quiet focus or one-on-one interactions.

并非每个人都觉得主动搭话、周旋于社交场很容易，尤其当你更偏内向时。那种“技术负责人应当时刻活跃社交”的期待，在你天性更偏好安静专注或一对一交流时，会让人喘不过气。

But being introverted doesn't mean you can't build strong relationships; it just means your approach may look different. You might skip the big team lunches and instead build rapport during recurring one-on-ones. You might not jump into every Slack thread, but when you do, you add thoughtful insight. You may not talk the most in meetings, but when you speak, people listen.

但内向并不意味着你无法建立牢固关系；它只是意味着你的做法看起来会不同。你可以跳过大型团队午餐，转而在定期一对一中建立融洽。你不必跳入每一个 Slack 串，但一旦加入，就给出有思考的见解。你在会上未必说得最多，但你一开口，大家就会听。

People often assume I'm an extrovert. I'm not. I don't get energized by frequent small talk or bouncing between group conversations; I need time away from people to recharge. But I show up and do it anyway, because building strong relationships is part of the job, and I've found ways to do it that still work for me. And I'm not alone. Some of the strongest tech leads I know are introverts. They earn trust through consistency, deep listening, and thoughtful questions that help others feel seen.

人们常常以为我是外向的人。我不是。频繁的寒暄、在各种小组对话间跳来跳去并不能给我能量；我需要远离人群来充电。但我还是会出现、去做这件事，因为建立牢固关系是工作的一部分，而且我找到了依然适合我的做法。而且我并不孤单。我认识的一些最优秀的技术负责人就是内向者。他们通过一致性、深度倾听、以及帮助别人感到被看见的、有思考的问题，赢得信任。

If you're introverted, here are a few strategies that can help:

如果你内向，下面几个策略可能有帮助：

  • Leverage one-on-ones — These offer a quieter, more focused setting for building trust. You don't have to perform or think on your feet the same way you might in a group setting. Use these conversations to ask meaningful questions, check in on goals or concerns, and share feedback in a way that feels more natural than speaking up in a crowd.用好一对一——它们提供了一个更安静、更聚焦的建立信任的场合。你不必像在群体场合那样表现、临场发挥。利用这些对话提出有意义的问题、关心目标或顾虑、并以比在人群中发言更自然的方式分享反馈。
  • Prepare, prepare, and then prepare some more — Many introverts feel more confident when they've had time to gather their thoughts. Before meetings or conversations, jot down key points you want to raise, questions you want to ask, or updates to share. This preparation helps you show up more clearly and assertively, even if the setting isn't your comfort zone.准备、准备、再准备——很多内向者在有时间整理思路后会更有信心。在会议或对话之前，草草记下你想提出的要点、想问的问题、或想分享的更新。这种准备帮你更清晰、更有底气地出现，哪怕场合不在你的舒适区。
— PDF p.99 —
  • Use async communication to your advantage — You don't always need to speak up in real time. Writing a thoughtful message in Slack, leaving comments in a document, or summarizing your thinking in an email can build your visibility and influence. Written communication lets you contribute on your terms without the pressure of having to respond instantly.利用异步沟通为你加分——你不必总是实时开口。在 Slack 里写一条有思考的消息、在文档里留评论、或在邮件里总结你的思考，都能建立你的可见度和影响力。书面沟通让你按自己的节奏贡献，而不必承受必须即时回应的压力。
  • Set boundaries and recharge — As an introvert, your energy is finite, especially in high-interaction roles. Block out time for deep work, avoid back-to-back meetings when possible, and take short breaks to reset. When you protect your energy, you'll show up more present and intentional in the interactions that truly matter.设定边界、给自己充电——作为内向者，你的精力是有限的，尤其在高互动的岗位上。为深度工作留出整块时间、尽可能避免背靠背开会、并短暂休息来重置。当你保护好自己的精力，你会在真正重要的互动中更投入、更有意。

You don't need to change your personality to succeed as a tech lead. You can definitely be a great tech lead as an introvert. You just need to find a rhythm that works for you and start with the relationships that matter most.

作为技术负责人要成功，你不必改变自己的性格。内向者完全可以成为出色的技术负责人。你只需要找到一种适合自己的节奏，并从最重要的关系着手。

Key Takeaway本章要点

Building relationships is about creating the conditions where collaboration, trust, and leadership can thrive. You don't have to become someone you're not, and you don't have to get it perfect. What matters is that you show up with intention, curiosity, and consistency.

经营关系，就是创造让协作、信任和领导力得以蓬勃生长的条件。你不必变成另一个人，也不必做到完美。重要的是你带着意图、好奇和一致性出现。

Not every conversation will land, and not every relationship will click, but over time, your willingness to invest will shape how people experience working with you.

不是每次对话都能奏效，也不是每段关系都能一拍即合，但久而久之，你愿意投入的态度，会塑造别人与你共事时的体验。

So pick a place to start. Reach out. Ask questions. Listen well. And remem-ber that building relationships is a shared effort. It's a two-way street. Use these strategies to connect, but also recognize that the other person has to meet you halfway. All you can do is give it your best effort.

所以，挑一个地方开始吧。主动联系。提出问题。好好倾听。并记住：经营关系是共同的努力，是一条双向的路。用这些策略去建立连接，但也要认识到对方也必须主动向你走近。你所能做的，就是全力以赴。
